prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength lattice concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. The round-1 exchange tested it on the points I asked to have tested and it held. Five members now give the same account of the science: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime with the lattice light shift cancelled, and Ye's group realized it at systematic uncertainties near 1e-18 and showed millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a sample. That performance has been reproduced at RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL with agreed international comparisons, so this is a result measured against an external standard and not an interpretation under dispute. The chair's question on wording has a workable answer: the citation should name the lattice concept and the 1e-18 realization, and say nothing about frequency combs or single-ion control, which keeps it separate from 2005 and 2012. The credit fits two names and does not force anyone out under the three-person limit. As an experimentalist, I weigh that a measurement capability is not a new phenomenon, but the lattice clock has already moved from capability to use in relativistic geodesy, constraints on varying constants and dark-matter searches, so the payoff is demonstrated rather than promised.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I have not argued them away. First, 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control) mean the committee must accept that the neutral-atom lattice is a distinct step and not a refinement; I think it is, because the comb counts optical cycles and the lattice clock is the many-atom system that is counted, but I accept that this is a judgment and some colleagues will weigh it differently. Second, the line between inventor and refiner is contestable: the Paris lattice work, PTB and NIST groups, Ludlow and Lemke, and the single-ion clock community reached comparable uncertainties, and nobody has stated a principled line from the supplied evidence beyond concept (Katori) and performance leadership (Ye). Third, the SI redefinition of the second is still pending. Fourth, B006 is a larger and younger scientific wave, and a configuration that omits it should say why: for me the reason is an unresolved mechanism for the superconducting and correlated states and an incomplete credit, not a doubt about the observations.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B006 as his preferred prize for a concrete prediction followed by an unexpected experimental result, argues that the discovery of the phases does not depend on the unresolved pairing mechanism, and asks what the lattice clock has taught us about nature rather than how precisely it measures.
responses.response: The distinction between prediction and surprise is a fair test and I do not dismiss it. On the clock the answer is that it has already given measurements of nature: gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale atomic sample, and bounds on variation of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark-matter couplings that exceed what earlier clocks allowed. These are existing results, not prospects. I agree with him that the phases in B006 can be reported without a mechanism, and I do not call the observations premature. What holds me back is that the citation would have to avoid the mechanism while the credit leaves out Cao and the wider moire experimental and theoretical community, whereas B015 has a stable interpretation and a clean two-name credit. I keep B006 as my first alternative, and if the committee prefers a two-part configuration I would want B006 weighed seriously, but I do not move it ahead of B015 this year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B055 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the more conceptually settled and mature case, with about two decades of confirmation, while granting that B015 would beat B055 on credit cleanliness and not on scientific reach.
responses.response: I take the maturity and influence argument for B055 seriously, and I have moved it into my alternatives because of it. My difficulty is the one he states himself: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who told Molenkamp's group where to look, as well as Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy and the ARPES work, are outside the three supplied names, and the committee would be explaining that choice each year thereafter. He also notes that the promised dissipationless edge transport has not materialised, so the case rests on conceptual influence. I would not call the lattice clock narrower in reach, since it feeds geodesy, constants searches and the second itself, but I accept that this comparison is a matter of judgment and not of fact. If the committee's weight on conceptual organising principles exceeds its weight on clean credit, B055 is the candidate I would move to, not B010 or B037.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether a configuration omitting B006 needs a principled reason, whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with a condensed-matter candidate should be explored, and whether the SI redefinition of the second is a precondition.
responses.response: On B006, yes, I think a principled reason is owed, and I have given it above: an open mechanism and incomplete credit, with observations I accept. On a two-part prize, I considered pairing B015 with B006, but the three-person limit would be exhausted by the two clock names and force a truncation of the moire credit to one person, which would break the theory-plus-experiment pairing that makes B006 coherent. I would not support B015 plus B006 with a single moire name. A two-part configuration with B055 has the same problem on credit. On the SI second, I treat redefinition as a supporting consideration, not a precondition: the prize recognizes the invention and its realization, which are complete, and the redefinition depends on international metrology bodies, not on a further scientific result.

responses.point: Lindroth rests B015 on a distinct step from the 2005 comb prize and raises the single-ion, Paris and PTB/NIST contributions, and in round 1 resists treating B010 as a companion because of attribution trouble.
responses.response: I agree with her that single-ion clocks are the real edge of the credit, and her round-1 point that a narrowly framed lattice citation could look as if it neglects the ion lineage is the one I most want the citation to avoid. Wording the citation around the lattice concept and its realization, without the words 'optical clocks' in general, keeps it accurate, because the ion clocks reached their uncertainties by a different route and their principal recognition is the 2012 prize. I also agree with her objection to pairing with B010: Cirac, Zoller, Blatt and the lattice-simulation strand form at least two achievements, and the three-name limit would reopen the attribution disputes that make B015 attractive. Her caution that two atomic-physics first places should be tested with members from other fields has been met: Mehlig, Olsson and I moved toward B015 from other starting points.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the neutral-atom lattice clock is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, since that depends on a judgment I cannot settle by evidence alone.

Whether the Paris, PTB and NIST lattice contributions and the single-ion clock community justify a different credit than Katori and Ye; no member has stated a firm line between inventor and refiner on the supplied material.
Whether the committee will treat the pending SI redefinition of the second as a reason to wait; I judge it a supporting consideration only.
Whether B006 or B055 will be judged mature enough for a later year once the correlated-phase mechanism or the credit questions are better resolved.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or any credited name in B015, and my profile records no collaboration or institutional link to them. My PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur work is astroparticle physics, so I keep the field-adjacent disclosure on B007 (IceCube) and, through my CERN-based doctoral training, on B037 (Higgs); neither is in my preferred configuration, and I would disclose or step back if either were weighed seriously. I do not regard this disclosure as affecting B015, B006 or B055.
